scenarios.title: Wake Up the Outpost
scenarios.description: Welcome, Commander! Your crew has just landed. The Sun is shining on the solar panels and the batteries are not full yet. What should the outpost do first?

decisions.title: Start the science lab
decisions.explanation: Turn on the lab right away and start research.

decisions.title: Aim the panels at the Sun
decisions.explanation: Two astronauts go outside and tilt the panels to catch more light.

fact.text: Solar panels only make electricity when sunlight hits them, and they work best when they face the Sun. On the real Moon, one day lasts about two Earth weeks, and so does one night! We made them shorter in this game.

scenarios.title: Dusty Panels
scenarios.description: Your landing kicked up lots of Moon dust, and now it's covering the solar panels. Dusty panels make less power.

decisions.title: Go outside and clean them
decisions.explanation: Two astronauts put on spacesuits and wipe the panels.

decisions.title: Leave the dust for now
decisions.explanation: Stay safe inside. The panels will charge more slowly.
decisions.laterHint: Panels will charge slower every day

fact.text: Moon dust is sharp like tiny bits of glass and sticks to everything. Apollo astronauts found it on their suits, their tools and even inside their spacecraft.

scenarios.title: Seeds from Earth
scenarios.description: You brought a box of seeds from Earth! Plants make oxygen and food, but they need warm lights, and lights need power.

decisions.title: Plant a space garden
decisions.explanation: Set up grow lights and plant the seeds.

decisions.title: Keep the seeds packed
decisions.explanation: Save the power for other systems.
decisions.laterHint: No fresh food or oxygen later

fact.text: In 2022, NASA-funded scientists grew small plants in real Moon soil that Apollo astronauts brought back. On the Space Station, astronauts have grown and eaten their own lettuce!

scenarios.title: Build a Shield
scenarios.description: Mission Control says the Sun is getting busy. The Moon has no thick air to protect you from space radiation. You can make the shelter safer by piling Moon soil on top of it.

decisions.title: Pile soil on the shelter
decisions.explanation: Use the rover to cover the shelter with thick Moon soil.
decisions.laterHint: Protects the crew in a future storm

decisions.title: Collect rock samples instead
decisions.explanation: Use today to gather interesting rocks.

fact.text: On Earth, our air and magnetic field block most space radiation. The Moon has neither. Radiation adds up in your body over time, so NASA plans how long astronauts can spend outside. A thick layer of Moon soil (called **regolith**) on top of a base can help block it.

scenarios.title: Crater Expedition
scenarios.description: Scientists on Earth spotted a big crater 3 km away with very old rocks on its edge. The trip is long, and the rover needs a lot of power.

decisions.title: Drive to the crater
decisions.explanation: A long rover trip to find the best rocks.

decisions.title: Search near the base
decisions.explanation: A short walk to collect rocks close by.

fact.text: Apollo astronauts brought 382 kg (842 lb) of Moon rocks and soil back to Earth. That's about as heavy as a grand piano! Scientists are still studying them today.

scenarios.title: Solar Storm Warning!
scenarios.description: Space weather alert! A big explosion on the Sun, called a **solar flare**, has just happened. Fast radiation particles might reach the Moon soon.

decisions.title: Everyone to the shelter
decisions.explanation: Stay safe inside the shelter until the storm passes.

decisions.title: Finish the experiment outside
decisions.explanation: Keep working. The experiment is almost done.

overrides.note: Your soil shield from Day 4 cut the radiation in half!

fact.text: In August 1972, a huge solar storm happened between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions. Luckily, no astronauts were on the Moon. Today NASA watches the Sun all the time so it can warn astronauts.

scenarios.title: Last Day of Sunlight
scenarios.description: Tomorrow the Sun sets and the long, cold lunar night begins. Your solar panels will stop working. How will you use the last sunny day?

decisions.title: Fill the batteries
decisions.explanation: Go outside to tilt the panels toward the low Sun, and switch off the lab.

decisions.title: Finish experiments before dark
decisions.explanation: Use the last sunlight to complete your research.

fact.text: A Moon night can get colder than −130 °C (−208 °F). That's colder than anywhere ever measured on Earth! Machines need heaters to survive.

scenarios.title: Night Falls
scenarios.description: It's dark and getting very cold. Heaters keep the outpost warm, but heaters use lots of battery power.

decisions.title: Heat the whole outpost
decisions.explanation: Keep the lab warm so night research can continue.

decisions.title: Heat only the habitat
decisions.explanation: Close the lab and keep the crew warm.

fact.text: Surviving the long lunar night is one of the hardest problems for a Moon base. NASA is developing small nuclear power systems that can make electricity day and night.

scenarios.title: Air Filter Alert
scenarios.description: Beep beep! The air filter that removes the gas we breathe out (**carbon dioxide**, CO₂) is getting clogged. The air is getting stuffy.

decisions.title: Install a new filter
decisions.explanation: Put in a fresh filter. The fan needs extra power.

decisions.title: Rest and breathe slowly
decisions.explanation: The crew rests today so they make less CO₂.

fact.text: On Apollo 13, the air filters stopped working. Engineers on Earth invented a fix using tape, plastic bags and cardboard, and the astronauts built it in space!

scenarios.title: Harvest Time!
scenarios.description: Your space garden is growing! The little plants are green and healthy. What will you do with them?

decisions.title: Let them keep growing
decisions.explanation: Plants keep making fresh oxygen, but grow lights use power.

decisions.title: Harvest them for science
decisions.explanation: Freeze the plants in the lab to study how they grew on the Moon.

fact.text: Plants take in the carbon dioxide we breathe out and give back oxygen. Future Moon and Mars bases will need gardens for both food and air.

scenarios.title: Running Low on Air
scenarios.description: The oxygen tanks are emptying faster than planned. Without plants, the crew has to make oxygen another way.

decisions.title: Split water to make oxygen
decisions.explanation: A machine uses electricity to turn water into oxygen.

decisions.title: Rest in the warm habitat
decisions.explanation: Less work means less oxygen used, but the heaters run longer.

fact.text: The International Space Station makes oxygen by using electricity to split water (H₂O) into hydrogen and oxygen. This is called **electrolysis**.

scenarios.title: Moonquake!
scenarios.description: The ground is shaking! Your **seismometer** (a machine that feels vibrations) detected a **moonquake**.

decisions.title: Check every module outside
decisions.explanation: Walk around the outpost to look for damage and measure the shaking.

decisions.title: Stay inside and record data
decisions.explanation: Let the instruments collect the data safely.

fact.text: Apollo astronauts left seismometers on the Moon. They recorded moonquakes, and some shook for up to 10 minutes!

scenarios.title: Tiny Space Rock Hit
scenarios.description: A tiny space rock, smaller than a pea, hit a power cable! Some electricity is leaking away.

decisions.title: Repair it outside
decisions.explanation: An astronaut goes out in the cold and dark to fix it.

decisions.title: Use the backup cable
decisions.explanation: Send power through a longer backup cable, but some power is lost.

fact.text: Without air to burn them up, tiny space rocks called **micrometeorites** hit the Moon's surface all the time.

scenarios.title: Call Home
scenarios.description: It's time to send your science results to Earth. The big antenna needs a lot of power to send all the data.

decisions.title: Send all the data
decisions.explanation: Scientists on Earth get all your discoveries.

decisions.title: Send a short message
decisions.explanation: Send only the most important results and save power.

fact.text: A radio message takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth. From Mars it takes about 5 to 20 minutes, so astronauts on Mars can't have a normal phone call with Earth!

scenarios.title: Ice in the Shadows
scenarios.description: A spacecraft circling the Moon found signs of frozen water in a dark crater nearby. Water can be used for drinking, making oxygen and even rocket fuel!

decisions.title: Drive to the crater and drill
decisions.explanation: A cold night trip with the rover to look for ice.

decisions.title: Study the maps from inside
decisions.explanation: Learn about the crater from spacecraft data, safe and warm.

fact.text: In 2009, NASA's LCROSS mission crashed a rocket into a dark crater near the Moon's south pole and found water ice in the cloud it kicked up!

scenarios.title: Sunrise Is Coming
scenarios.description: This is the last day of your mission! The Sun will rise soon and your ride home is on the way. Do you have enough energy left for one more experiment?

decisions.title: One last big experiment
decisions.explanation: Use the remaining power for one more discovery.

decisions.title: Pack up safely
decisions.explanation: Pack the samples carefully and save power.

fact.text: NASA's Artemis program plans to send astronauts to the Moon's south pole, where they will live and work for longer missions.

flagDailyEffects.note: Dusty panels made less power today.

debriefTips.lifeSupport: Every trip outside uses extra oxygen. Fresh air filters and plants can help!
debriefTips.power: At night there's no sunlight to recharge. Try saving power before Day 8!
debriefTips.radiation: Radiation adds up and never goes away. Stay in the shelter during solar storms!
